title: Dual-Order-Parameter Coupling Drives Plant-Community Diversity Formation Based on the Natural-Intrinsic-Intelligence-Transformation Simulation Model
content: The latitudinal gradient of plant diversity represents one of the most fundamental and longdebated classical scientific questions in global biogeography. For centuries, traditional hypotheses including the energy hypothesis, climatestability hypothesis and habitatheterogeneity hypothesis can only provide statistical descriptions of observed correlations. They lack a unified mathematical-mechanistic framework, cannot decouple the dual driving mechanisms of exogenous environmental constraints and endogenous species regulation, and are incapable of quantitative solution and cross-scale extrapolation. Based on the Natural-Intrinsic-Intelligence-Transformation (NIIT) simulation model, this study constructs a rigorously self-consistent theoretical system of coupled habitat-order-parameter and endogenous-order-parameter dynamics. Using functional-analysis and axiomatic-constraint methods, we formally define habitat degree-of-freedom (habitat order-parameter) and plant endogenous degree-of-freedom (endogenous order-parameter), and propose an original axiom for dual-order-parameter decoupling and diversity emergence. We clarify the underlying dynamical mechanism governing macroscale plant-diversity patterns: high habitat degree-of-freedom in tropical regions provides sufficient upper limits for niche capacity, accompanied by sufficient endogenous functional differentiation of species; the coupled two order-parameters jointly generate extremely high community diversity. Towards temperate and boreal zones, environmental thresholds deactivate effective habitat dimensions, habitat degree-of-freedom declines substantially, and species endogenous attributes converge. Dual constraints jointly produce decreasing diversity along latitudinal gradients. Validated by multi-gradient vegetation cases across tropical-temperate-boreal biomes, the proposed theory accurately reproduces global plant-diversity patterns and fills the critical gap of dynamical-mechanism support that existing statistical descriptions lack. Compared with recent relevant studies published in Nature, this work overcomes the limitations of purely phenomenological induction and achieves theoretical upgrading from empirical statistics to axiomatic, quantifiable, decouplable and extrapolatable frameworks. It provides a novel underlying mathematical paradigm for understanding the formation, maintenance and prediction of global vegetation-diversity patterns.
